area: Area V. Performance Maneuvers and Ground Reference Maneuvers
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain load factor, overbanking tendency, maneuvering speed and turn rate and radius, read the load factor chart, and fly a 360° steep turn at about 45° bank in both directions to ACS standards.
why: Steep turns build smooth, coordinated control and outside awareness [[24:210|AFH 10-1]]. Knowing load factors helps prevent two serious accident types: stalls from steep turns near the ground, and structural failures [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]].

prereading.what: Steep turns: forces, entry, rollout, common errors.
prereading.label: AFH Ch 10, 10-1 to 10-3

prereading.what: Shallow, medium and steep turns; coordination; slip and skid; turn radius; overbanking tendency; parallax.
prereading.label: AFH Ch 3, 3-12 to 3-15

prereading.what: Load factors, limit loads, the load factor chart, load factor and stall speed, VA.
prereading.label: PHAK Ch 5, 5-33 to 5-36

prereading.label: PHAK Ch 5, 5-38 to 5-41

warmup: In a level turn, you have to pull back to hold altitude. The steeper you bank, the harder you pull. Where does that extra pull go, and what do you think it does to your stall speed?

key_terms.def: A level 360° or 720° turn with a bank between 45° and 60° [[24:210|AFH 10-1]]. The ACS checkride uses about 45°.
The total load on the structure compared to the airplane's weight, measured in Gs. A load factor of 3 means the load is three times the weight [[1:130|PHAK 5-33]].
The highest load factor the airplane is designed for in normal use: 3.8 G for normal category [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]].
In a steep bank the outside wing flies faster and makes more lift, so the bank keeps steepening unless you hold opposite aileron [[24:75|AFH 3-14]].
The most speed at which the design limit load can be imposed by gusts or full deflection of one control without structural damage. It changes with weight [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]] [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]].
An older limit on some airplanes: the most speed at which, at any weight, full control travel won't exceed the design limit load factor [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].
A stall when the G-load is above +1G, like in a turn or pull-up. It happens at a higher airspeed than a normal stall [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].
Degrees of heading change per second [[1:135|PHAK 5-38]].
Aileron and rudder working together so the ball stays centered [[1:220|PHAK 8-18]].

chunks.title: What a steep turn is and why we fly it

body.p: A steep turn is one or more level 360° or 720° turns, in one or both directions, at a bank between 45° and 60° [[24:210|AFH 10-1]]. On the private checkride you fly about 45°, one way and then the other (ACS PA.V.A.S3, S4).
It trains smooth, coordinated control, awareness of where you are against outside references, split attention, and a constant scan for traffic [[24:210|AFH 10-1]].
Compared with normal turns, you will meet [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]:

bullets: Higher G-forces
Overbanking tendency
A big loss of vertical lift
Heavy back pressure on the elevator
A need for more power to hold altitude and airspeed

callout.text: The FAA says to start performance maneuvers with a detailed ground lesson, and only after the basics are solid [[24:210|AFH 10-1]]. That's this lesson.

check.q: What bank range does the AFH give for steep turns?

chunks.title: Load factor and the load factor chart

body.p: When you bank, total lift splits into a vertical part (holds you up) and a horizontal part (turns you). To stay level you raise the angle of attack so the vertical part still equals weight [[24:211|AFH 10-2]] [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].

In a level turn, load factor comes from two forces: gravity (weight) and centrifugal force [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]]. For a given bank in a level turn, every airplane gets the same load factor, no matter the speed [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

head: Level-turn bank
Load factor
Source
rows: 2 G (you and the airplane weigh double)
More than 3.8 G (past the normal category limit)

body.p: Read the chart: the line stays low at shallow banks, then rises at a terrific rate after 45° or 50° [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]]. It never reaches 90°, because a level turn at 90° bank is impossible [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]]. For the average GA airplane, about 60° is the most bank you can hold level; 10° more adds about 1 G [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]].

Limit loads from [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]]. The structure must also carry 1.5 times the limit load without failing, but parts may bend. That reserve is for surprises, not for using on purpose [[1:130|PHAK 5-33]].

callout.text: 45° = 1.4 G. 60° = 2 G. Past 60° the G's shoot up.

check.q: You hold a level 60° bank. How heavy do you and the airplane feel?

chunks.title: Accelerated stalls: why stall speed goes up

body.p: As load factor goes up, so does stall speed. Stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].
Example from [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. The stall speed rises about one-half at about 63° of bank [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]].

A stall above +1G is an accelerated stall. It usually happens by accident in poorly flown turns, steep pullouts, or an overshot base-to-final turn. It's typically demonstrated during steep turns [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

If the turn is coordinated, the nose pitches down like a normal stall. If not, the bank may change. Recover: forward elevator to cut the AOA, level the wings, coordinate with rudder, adjust power [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

callout.text: Accelerated stalls come at higher airspeeds or lower pitch than you expect and can surprise you. Failing to recover right away can lead to a spin [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

check.q: An airplane stalls at 50 knots wings level. About what speed will it stall in a level 45° turn?

body.p: Because of the higher load factors, fly steep turns at or below VA or VO [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. At or below VA or VO, the airplane stalls before it exceeds the design load limit [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

VA is the most speed at which the design limit load can be imposed by gusts or by full deflection of one control without structural damage [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]] [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]]. It must be in the AFM/POH of recently designed airplanes [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]].

callout.text: VA protects you only for one full control input, one time, in one axis, in smooth air. It does not protect you from several full inputs in one axis or full inputs in more than one axis at once [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]].

body.p: Weight matters. VA may be 100 knots when the airplane is heavy but only 90 knots when it's light [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]]. Extra weight raises stall speed [[1:246|PHAK 10-2]], and for older airplanes VA is about 1.7 times the normal stall speed [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]]. So a lighter airplane, with its lower stall speed, has a lower VA.

callout.text: Flying solo with half fuel? You're lighter than max gross, so the safe maneuvering speed may be lower than the number printed for max weight. Check your POH.

body.p: Checkride standard: use the manufacturer's recommended airspeed; if there isn't one, use an airspeed not above VA (ACS PA.V.A.S2). The actual numbers come from your POH.

check.q: Does VA go up or down as weight decreases?
check.a: Down. Example: 100 knots heavy, 90 knots light [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]].

head: Turn
Bank
What the airplane does
rows: Stability slowly levels the wings; hold aileron into the turn
Stays at the bank; neutral aileron
Keeps rolling into the bank; hold opposite aileron

body.p: Table from [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].
Why it overbanks: the outside wing travels a longer path in the same time, so it flies faster and makes more lift [[24:75|AFH 3-14]]. Hold opposite aileron once you reach your bank.

The faster outside wing also makes more drag, causing a slight slip. Fix it with rudder [[24:75|AFH 3-14]]. Watch the left-turning tendencies like P-factor too; they need good rudder and aileron teamwork [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

Check coordination with the ball. In a slip the ball moves to the inside of the turn; in a skid it moves to the outside [[1:220|PHAK 8-18]]. You also feel it: pushed to the outside in a skid, to the inside in a slip [[24:74|AFH 3-13]].

callout.text: Step on the ball: press the rudder on the side the ball is on [[1:220|PHAK 8-18]].
Uncoordinated flight can set up a spin [[24:73|AFH 3-12]]. A stall in a slipping or skidding turn can spin the airplane in the direction of the rudder, no matter which wing is up [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

check.q: You're holding 45° of bank and the bank keeps steepening. Why, and what do you do?
check.a: Overbanking tendency: the outside wing is faster and makes more lift. Hold opposite aileron and keep the ball centered with rudder [[24:75|AFH 3-14]] [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

body.p: At a given speed, more bank means a faster rate of turn. At a given bank, more speed means a slower rate and a bigger radius [[24:75|AFH 3-14]].

bullets: ROT (degrees per second) = 1,091 × tan(bank) ÷ true airspeed in knots [[1:135|PHAK 5-38]].
Example: 30° bank at 120 knots = 5.25° per second, about 68.6 seconds for a full circle [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]].
Same 30° bank at 240 knots = only about 2.62° per second [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]].
Radius = V² ÷ (11.26 × tan(bank)). At 120 knots and 30° bank, radius = 2,215 feet [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]].
At 240 knots and 30° bank, radius = 8,861 feet. Double the speed, four times the radius [[1:137|PHAK 5-40]] [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]].

callout.text: Airspeed is the biggest factor in how much room a turn takes. Many pilots have steepened the bank when simply slowing down would have been better [[1:138|PHAK 5-41]].

body.p: Steep turns use a high bank for max turning performance at a given speed [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. That's why they make tight, quick circles.

check.q: Same bank, airspeed doubles. What happens to the turn radius?

bullets: 1. Clear the area of traffic and other hazards [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. Some programs require two 90° clearing turns in opposite directions [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].
2. Pick a distant reference to know when to start the rollout [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. Note your entry heading and altitude.
3. Set the manufacturer's recommended entry speed, VA or VO [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. Numbers come from the POH.
4. Roll smoothly into the bank (about 45° for the private checkride). Generally before 30° of bank, smoothly add back pressure and add power [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].
5. At your bank, hold considerable back pressure to stay level [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. Hold opposite aileron against overbanking and keep the ball centered [[24:75|AFH 3-14]].
6. Trim is optional. If you use it, add up-trim and power as the bank steepens, and remember to take them out at the end [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

7. Look outside: watch both the nose and the wings against the horizon, not just the nose [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. Small pitch fixes with elevator; hold bank with aileron [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. Keep scanning for traffic [[24:212|AFH 10-3]].
8. Start rollout at half your bank angle before the entry heading. At 45°, start about 22° early. (AFH example: right turn from 270° at 60° bank, start rollout at 240°) [[24:212|AFH 10-3]].
9. While rolling out, ease off back pressure, trim and power to hold altitude and airspeed [[24:212|AFH 10-3]].
10. Roll straight into the turn the other way if the examiner asks (ACS PA.V.A.S4).

body.p: Also on the checkride: clear the area (ACS PA.V.A.S1), use the right airspeed (ACS PA.V.A.S2), roll into a coordinated 360° turn at about 45° bank (ACS PA.V.A.S3), and repeat in the other direction if asked (ACS PA.V.A.S4).

callout.text: Sitting left of center, the nose seems to rise in left turns and drop in right turns (parallax) [[24:76|AFH 3-15]]. Learn each direction's sight picture. And don't lean away from the turn [[24:76|AFH 3-15]].

check.q: You enter a left 45° steep turn on heading 090°. About when do you start rolling out?

body.p: Common steep turn errors [[24:212|AFH 10-3]]:

bullets: Not clearing the area; not scanning for traffic during the turn
Poor pitch control on entry or rollout; gaining or losing altitude
Not holding a constant bank; poor coordination
Poor use of trim or power; poor airspeed control
Becoming disoriented
Flying by the instruments instead of outside references
Starting the rollout too early, or not stopping on the heading

body.p: Altitude is the main error. It's common to let the nose drop and lose a lot of altitude fast [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

callout.text: Nose low and losing altitude? First shallow the bank with coordinated opposite aileron and rudder, THEN raise the nose with back pressure. Pulling only on the elevator steepens the bank and overstresses the airplane [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

body.p: The high G's and the yaw that feels like motion toward and away from the ground can be confusing at first [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. Expect it, keep your eyes outside, and the feeling fades with practice.

check.q: In a steep turn the nose has dropped and you're losing altitude fast. What do you do first?
check.a: Reduce the bank with coordinated opposite aileron and rudder, then raise the nose [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

chunks.title: Risk: traffic, low altitude and distraction

body.p: Collision hazards. Clear before every turn and every training maneuver. Clearing turns plus good scanning are the best collision-avoidance strategy [[24:33|AFH 1-12]]. In training, call out "clear" left, right, above, below. In a high-wing, raise the wing toward the turn and look; in a low-wing, lower it and look [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15]] [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]].
High wings block your view above; low wings block below. Banking now and then uncovers blind spots [[16:13|AC 90-48E 12.1]]. In a steep turn, the high wing hides a big piece of sky, so keep looking.

Low altitude. The sudden loss of control in a steep turn or abrupt back pressure near the ground has caused many accidents [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]]. Loss of control in flight and CFIT are two of the top four causes of fatal GA accidents [[30:22|RMH 3-4]]. Practice steep turns high enough to recover from a stall or spin.

Distraction and orientation. A distraction can pull your attention off flying and scanning, and work overload can make you fixate on one thing [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. Split your attention: outside picture, quick instrument cross-check, traffic, back outside.

callout.text: With a passenger aboard, no intentional bank over 60° unless everyone wears an approved parachute. Flight tests and CFI instruction on required maneuvers are exempt [[35:416|14 CFR 91.307]].

body.p: Uncoordinated flight. Keep the ball centered. A skid near the stall is a setup for a spin [[24:127|AFH 5-22]] [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

check.q: Name two ways to clear the area before steep turns.
check.a: Clearing turns (for example two 90° turns in opposite directions) [[24:33|AFH 1-12]], and calling "clear" left, right, above and below while lifting or lowering a wing to look [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15]] [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]].

scenario.title: Steep turns on a busy practice-area afternoon
scenario.setup: You're solo in a high-wing trainer, half fuel, in the local practice area. Two other trainers are working nearby. Clouds keep you lower than you'd like. Halfway through a left steep turn, the radio gets busy and you glance at your tablet to check where the other airplanes are. When you look up, the nose is below the horizon, the bank is past 55°, and the altimeter is unwinding.

questions.q: Before you started, what should you have done about the other trainers?
questions.a: Clear the area with clearing turns and a good scan, calling "clear" left, right, above, below [[24:33|AFH 1-12]] [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15]]. In a high-wing, raise the wing toward the turn and look [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]].

questions.q: You're solo with half fuel. Does that change your entry speed?
questions.a: Possibly. VA drops as weight drops (example: 100 knots heavy, 90 knots light) [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]]. Use the POH's recommended speed or one not above VA for your weight.

questions.q: The nose is low, bank steep, altitude falling. How do you recover?
questions.a: Shallow the bank first with coordinated opposite aileron and rudder, then raise the nose. Pulling only on the elevator steepens the bank and overstresses the airplane [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

questions.q: What caused this, and how do you prevent it?
questions.a: A distraction pulled your eyes inside [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. Keep your eyes mostly outside on the nose and wings against the horizon [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]; deal with the radio or tablet after rolling out.

questions.q: The clouds push you low. Why is that a problem for steep turns?
questions.a: Higher load factor raises stall speed; a stall or loss of control in a steep turn near the ground has caused many accidents [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]]. If you can't get enough altitude, skip the steep turns today.

questions.q: You notice the ball is out toward the inside of the turn. What's happening and what do you do?
questions.a: A slip. Step on the ball: add rudder on the side the ball is on [[1:220|PHAK 8-18]]. Stalling uncoordinated can lead to a spin [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

skills.practice: Do two 90° clearing turns in opposite directions, or your CFI's method, every time [[24:33|AFH 1-12]]. Say "clear" out loud [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15]].

skills.do: Set the manufacturer's recommended airspeed, or one not above VA.
skills.practice: Learn the POH entry speed and VA for your weight [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]]. Practice setting the power that gives that speed in level flight before you roll in.

skills.do: Roll into a coordinated 360° turn at about 45° bank.
skills.practice: Add back pressure and power before 30° of bank [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. Learn the 45° sight picture of the cowling against the horizon [[24:76|AFH 3-15]], then cross-check the attitude indicator.

skills.do: Fly the turn in the other direction when asked.
skills.practice: Practice left and right back to back. The sight picture differs: the nose seems higher in left turns and lower in right turns [[24:76|AFH 3-15]].

skills.do: Hold entry altitude ±100 feet, airspeed ±10 knots, bank ±5°, and roll out on the entry heading ±10° (ACS PA.V.A.S5).
skills.practice: Lead the rollout by half the bank angle [[24:212|AFH 10-3]]. Watch nose and wings against the horizon for altitude [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. Chair-fly the sequence at home.

quiz.q: What is the load factor in a level, coordinated 45° bank turn?
quiz.why: A level 45° banked turn gives a load factor of 1.41 [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

quiz.q: An airplane stalls at 50 knots in level flight. What is its stall speed in a level 60° bank turn?
quiz.why: It stalls at 70 knots at 60°; stall speed rises with the square root of load factor [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

quiz.q: What causes the overbanking tendency in a steep turn?
options: Adverse yaw from the down aileron
The outside wing flies faster and makes more lift
The inside wing has a higher angle of attack
quiz.why: The outside wing travels a longer path in the same time, so it's faster and makes more lift [[24:75|AFH 3-14]].

quiz.q: How does VA change as the airplane gets lighter?
quiz.why: VA may be 100 knots heavy but only 90 knots light [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]].

quiz.q: In a steep turn the nose is low and altitude is dropping fast. What should you do first?
options: Pull back hard on the elevator
Reduce bank with coordinated aileron and rudder, then raise the nose
Add more bank to tighten the turn
quiz.why: Shallow the bank first, then add back pressure. Elevator alone steepens the bank and overstresses the airplane [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

quiz.q: You start a right 60° steep turn on heading 270°. Using the AFH rule of thumb, where do you begin the rollout?
quiz.why: Lead by half the bank: 30° early, at 240° [[24:212|AFH 10-3]].

quiz.q: At a constant bank angle, airspeed doubles. The turn radius becomes:
quiz.why: Radius goes with speed squared: double the speed, four times the radius [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]].

quiz.q: What is the limit load factor for a normal category airplane?
quiz.why: Normal category is 3.8 to -1.52 [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]]. A level 75° bank exceeds 3.8 [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

takeaways: Steep turn checkride: about 45° bank, ±100 ft, ±10 knots, ±5° bank, roll out ±10° (ACS PA.V.A.S5).
45° = 1.41 G, 60° = 2 G; stall speed rises with the square root of load factor [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].
Fly at or below the POH speed or VA; VA goes down when the airplane is lighter [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]].
Hold opposite aileron against overbanking and keep the ball centered [[24:75|AFH 3-14]] [[1:220|PHAK 8-18]].
Nose low? Shallow the bank first, then pull [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].
Clear the area and keep scanning outside the whole time [[24:212|AFH 10-3]].
cfi_notes: Teach on the ground first, then build in steps with enough repetition, per the AFH [[24:210|AFH 10-1]].
Altitude loss from a dropping nose is the main error; students often look only at the nose. Have them watch nose and wings [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].
Students who fix a nose-low steep turn with elevator only tighten the spiral. Drill 'bank first, then pitch' [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].
Point out parallax: left and right turns look different from the left seat [[24:76|AFH 3-15]]. Watch for students leaning away from the turn [[24:76|AFH 3-15]].
If trim is used, check that it and the extra power come out on rollout [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].
Examiners often ask about VA vs weight, the load factor chart, and why stall speed rises in a turn. Have the student read 45° and 60° off Figure 5-53.
Ask the student to verbalize 'clear' and keep scanning during the turn; failing to scan is a listed error [[24:212|AFH 10-3]] [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15]].
gaps: Entry speed, VA/VO at various weights, and power settings are airplane-specific: use the POH/AFM.
The sources give no minimum altitude for practicing steep turns. 14 CFR 91.303's 1,500 ft AGL rule is for aerobatic flight, which a 45° steep turn normally is not; use the CFI's or school's minimum.
The sources state that VA drops with weight (100 vs 90 knot example) but don't fully explain why; the lesson links it to lower stall speed at lower weight using PHAK 10-2 and PHAK 5-35.
The ACS bank for private pilots (about 45°) comes from the ACS itself, not the handbooks (which say 45° to 60°).
